rows.title: Effects of Aromatherapy on Stress and Anxiety Among Intensive Care Unit Nurses: A Systematic Review.
rows.discovery_query: ((ashwagandha[Title/Abstract] OR theanine[Title/Abstract] OR kava[Title/Abstract] OR lavender[Title/Abstract] OR chamomile[Title/Abstract] OR rhodiola[Title/Abstract] OR magnesium[Title/Abstract] OR aromatherapy[Title/Abstract]) AND (stress[Title/Abstract] OR anxiety[Title/Abstract] OR anxious[Title/Abstract])) AND 2022:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text] NOT retracted publication[pt] NOT case reports[pt]
rows.abstract: Nurses working in intensive care units (ICU) are at high risk for stress and anxiety. Aromatherapy stands out as a non-pharmacological and easily implementable complementary approach for alleviating these symptoms. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic review specifically examining the effects of aromatherapy on stress and anxiety among ICU nurses. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the effects of aromatherapy on stress and anxiety among ICU nurses and to assess the methodological quality of the evidence. In this systematic review, a literature search was conducted in the Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science and Cochrane Library databases without any time restrictions. The review includes randomised controlled, experimental and quasi-experimental studies evaluating the effects of aromatherapy interventions on stress and/or anxiety among ICU nurses. The selection of studies, data extraction and assessment of methodological quality were conducted independently by two researchers. This systematic review included five studies involving a total of 254 participants. Two of these studies are randomised controlled trials, and three are quasi-experimental studies. The studies included in the review demonstrate that aromatherapy is administered using various essential oils and application methods (inhalation, topical application, etc.). The findings suggest that aromatherapy interventions may reduce stress among ICU nurses, whereas evidence regarding anxiety reduction is mixed and less consistent across studies. Aromatherapy may have potential benefits for reducing stress among ICU nurses, whereas evidence for anxiety reduction remains limited and inconsistent. Further high-quality studies are needed before firm conclusions or routine clinical implementation can be recommended. Aromatherapy may be considered as an optional supportive intervention within staff well-being programs, provided that safety, scent sensitivity, infection-control procedures and individual preferences are taken into account. However, standardised protocols and further high-quality evidence are required to support its routine clinical use.

rows.title: Aromatherapy for Anxiety and Pain in Radiologic and Interventional Procedures a Scoping Review.

rows.abstract: To describe the scope of evidence on the use and effects of aromatherapy for reducing anxiety and pain in adults undergoing radiologic and interventional procedures. Scoping review guided by the Arksey and O'Malley framework and reported using PRISMA‑ScR guidelines. A comprehensive search of PubMed, Scopus, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Library was conducted for studies published between 2013 and 2025. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cohort studies, case series, or pilot studies involving adults receiving an aromatherapy intervention during a diagnostic or interventional radiology procedure, with anxiety and/or pain as outcomes. Twenty-six RCTs met inclusion criteria. Data extraction captured essential oil (EO) type, delivery method, exposure duration, outcome measures, and main findings. Lavender was the most frequently studied EO, followed by peppermint, rose-based oils, citrus oils, chamomile, clary sage, Osmanthus fragrans, and Cananga odorata. EO's were delivered using cotton balls, gauze, aromatherapy tabs, patches, masks, inhalers, and diffusers. Anxiety was more frequently evaluated than pain. Reductions in anxiety were commonly reported, particularly in studies using lavender-based interventions, while findings related to pain were more variable. Marked heterogeneity in EO composition, delivery approaches, procedures, and outcome measurement tools limit cross-study comparison and generalizability. Aromatherapy, particularly lavender, may reduce procedural anxiety, while evidence supporting pain reduction remains limited. Substantial methodological variability highlights the need for standardized protocols, transparent reporting of EO composition, and rigorous study designs to clarify clinical utility. Consistent with the American Society for Pain Management Nursing's emphasis on integrative, evidence-based care, aromatherapy may serve as a safe, nonpharmacologic adjunct to support patient well-being, particularly for procedural anxiety. Safe implementation requires nursing competency in EO selection, delivery methods, contraindications, and patient screening. Continued nursing leadership and advocacy are essential to advance multimodal, patient-centered approaches to procedural pain and anxiety management across care settings.
